strengths: First principled, unbiased, and tractable RL algorithm for diffusion language models, addressing a genuine gap in the literature
Sound mathematical framework: reformulating GRPO's token sum as timestep expectation enables unbiased Monte Carlo estimation with theoretical justification
Well-reasoned critique of prior work (diffu-GRPO, UniGRPO) identifying how heuristic approximations introduce bias inconsistent with RL assumptions
Consistent empirical improvements across three distinct mathematical reasoning tasks with notable compute-quality tradeoffs (4x speedup at equivalent performance)
Excellent practical engineering: clear algorithm pseudocode, comprehensive implementation details, proper handling of caching, EOS tokens, and numerical stability
Transparent discussion of limitations and concrete practical considerations that demonstrate careful engineering
Well-structured presentation with effective use of figures and clear background material on diffusion language models
weaknesses: Mathematical justification for |o_i| ↔ m equivalence is unclear when multiple tokens are unmasked per step; the formal legitimacy of this replacement needs rigorous treatment
Lacks theoretical guarantees: no convergence analysis, variance bounds, or formal proof that AGRPO recovers GRPO as k→m despite unbiasedness claims
Limited experimental scope: only three math/reasoning tasks from a single base model (LLaDA-8B); no ablations on k, low-discrepancy sampling utility, or evaluation on diverse domains
Entropy collapse issue dismissed as minor limitation despite being described as a critical failure mode with reduced diversity and formulaic outputs; deserves investigation and mitigation strategies
Significant performance gaps persist vs. autoregressive GRPO (MATH: 40.8% vs. 51.7%), limiting practical impact despite comparable relative gains
Questionable baseline results where CoT SFT decreases performance on GSM8K/MATH for diffusion models (e.g., 79.8→78.8) without explanation
Missing ablations and analysis: no validation that low-discrepancy sampling reduces variance empirically, no wall-clock time comparisons, no convergence criteria specified
Incomplete prior work comparisons: UniGRPO results missing for Countdown task; limited dLLM RL baselines available
Fixed context length limitation inadequately addressed despite being fundamental constraint vs. autoregressive models; BlockDiff alternative dismissed without justification
No code release mentioned and insufficient computational cost reporting to fully assess reproducibility despite adequate hyperparameter documentation

strengths: Novel and well-motivated multi-step MDP formulation for dLLM post-training that enables unbiased policy gradients without ELBO approximations
Rigorous theoretical framework with formal proof of unbiasedness (Theorem A.1) and principled variance reduction techniques
Thorough experimental validation with consistent improvements over comparable dLLM RL methods across four reasoning tasks
Valuable novel analysis showing post-trained models can sample 4x faster with minimal performance loss, opening new inference/quality tradeoffs
Excellent reproducibility practices with extensive implementation details and commitment to release code
Strong ablations studies demonstrating effects of MC samples (k) and variance reduction techniques on convergence and stability
weaknesses: Significant performance gap on harder tasks (MATH: 42.0% vs 51.7% for GRPO) with insufficient investigation; counterintuitive finding that GSM8K-trained models outperform MATH-trained models deserves deeper analysis
20% computational overhead per gradient step compared to diffu-GRPO/SPG (Table 2) inadequately justified; claimed amortization via rollout generation dominance lacks empirical evidence
Entropy importance sampling design (Section 4.2.2) lacks rigorous theoretical justification; appears ad-hoc despite maintaining unbiasedness, and ablation shows only modest convergence improvements
Acknowledged entropy collapse (Remark G.1) producing formulaic, low-diversity outputs with no proposed solutions, limiting practical applicability for reasoning tasks
Fundamental dLLM limitations persist and largely unaddressed: fixed sequence length (impractical), slow inference without KV caching (Appendix F), still significantly lag AR models
Limited evaluation scope: only LLaDA-8B; scalability to larger models and non-reasoning RL tasks unclear; unclear when practitioners should choose dLLMs+AGRPO over AR alternatives
Baseline comparisons for competing methods taken from papers rather than reproduced; improvements partly reflect better parsing/prompting rather than algorithmic superiority (Table 3)
Design choice of k≈m/4 optimality lacks theoretical analysis; variance reduction impact is primarily on convergence speed rather than final performance

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical framework: The multi-step MDP formulation elegantly sidesteps intractable sequence-level likelihoods, providing unbiased policy gradient estimates (Theorem A.1) in contrast to prior ELBO-based methods

Strong empirical results across diverse reasoning tasks: Substantial absolute improvements (+9.9% GSM8K, +4.6% MATH-500, +59.4% Countdown, +69.7% Sudoku) with comprehensive ablations validating design choices (k sensitivity, variance reduction techniques)

Novel inference compute/quality analysis: Demonstration that AGRPO-trained models achieve 4x faster sampling with minimal performance loss, a practically valuable contribution often overlooked in reasoning RL literature

Comprehensive practical engineering: Extensive implementation details (state caching, memory-efficient gradient accumulation, float64 sampling, EOS handling) and variance reduction techniques make the multi-step approach tractable
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear paper structure with effective figures (especially Figure 1), detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core concept: The multi-step MDP formulation for diffusion models exists in prior work (DDPO, Flow-GRPO for image generation); primary novelty is empirical validation on language, which is incremental

Computational overhead unresolved: Table 2 shows AGRPO incurs ~21% higher wall-clock cost per step vs competitive baselines (53.3s vs 43.8-44.6s); while inference dominates overall training time, the per-step overhead remains non-trivial and may accumulate

Persistent performance gap to autoregressive models: On MATH-500, AGRPO achieves 42.0% vs 51.7% for AR GRPO (9.7% gap); gaps widen on harder tasks despite motivation to close this gap; suboptimal MATH training (Section B.2 uses GSM8K model for MATH-500 results) suggests method limitations

Evaluation limited to single scale: Only 8B base model tested; generalization to 70B+ models and impact of scaling unclear; fundamental limitations unaddressed (no KV caching for dLLMs inherently limits inference speed vs AR models, per Appendix F)

Experimental concerns and baseline variation: Reported LLaDA-8B-Instruct baselines vary across prior work (76.7-79.9%, Table 3) making absolute comparisons noisier; limited direct mechanistic comparison to concurrent SPG method despite both avoiding sequence-level approximations; entropy collapse issue (Remark G.1) not thoroughly explored for downstream impact

Incomplete analysis of generalization: Models trained on single configuration (n=384, m=128) yet evaluated on vastly different settings (m=32-192); while robustness is impressive, underlying mechanism not explained; entropy importance sampling benefits unclear beyond reasoning tasks

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of sequence-level ELBO approximations in dLLM RL; principled step-level MDP formulation grounded in diffusion theory
Unbiased gradient estimation via Monte Carlo timestep sampling (Theorem A.1) is mathematically sound and makes step-level training practical
Valuable inference efficiency analysis demonstrating 4× speedup while maintaining performance, opening new perspective on amortizing training costs unique to dLLMs
Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablations on sampling budget k, variance reduction techniques, denoising steps, and unmasking strategies
Strong empirical results showing consistent improvements over existing dLLM RL methods (diffu-GRPO, VRPO, SPG) across multiple reasoning tasks
Thorough implementation documentation (Appendix F) and promised code release enhance reproducibility
Clear presentation of key conceptual differences via Figure 1 and logical progression of ideas
weaknesses: Critical issue with checkpoint selection methodology: selecting from 'last 150 steps and reporting best accuracy' constitutes overfitting to test set; should use validation-based selection only
Inconsistent baseline numbers across papers (Table 2) raise trustworthiness concerns; LLaDA-8B-Instruct baselines sometimes notably stronger than prior work reports
Marginal or no improvements on some tasks: MATH-500 at n=256 shows 0% gain over SPG; gains on MATH are modest despite claims of consistent outperformance
Train-test mismatch in action definitions: training uses random unmasking while inference uses confidence-based; while Table 3 shows some robustness, theoretical implications unclear
Still substantially behind AR models on harder tasks (MATH: 42.0% vs DeepSeekMath-RL 51.7%); limited analysis of why dLLMs struggle on harder reasoning

Limited conceptual novelty: step-level MDP formulation builds directly on established continuous diffusion RL (DDPO, Flow-GRPO); DCoLT already uses similar stepping with main difference being MC sampling efficiency
No formal convergence analysis or convergence rate guarantees despite using policy gradient methods
Variance reduction techniques (Section 4.2.2) show faster convergence (Figure 4) but similar final performance; practical benefits for final model quality unclear
Optimal sampling budget k ≈ m/4 derived from limited ablations with strong simplifying assumptions; generality to other tasks/scales unvalidated
Evaluation limited to 4 mathematical/constraint reasoning tasks; missing natural language reasoning, writing, or other domains
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; unclear if modest improvements are within noise
Only tested on 8B models; scaling properties to larger models unknown
Wall-time overhead of AGRPO (53.3s vs 43.8s for diffu-GRPO, +22%) not adequately discussed in main results despite claimed efficiency gains

strengths: Well-motivated principled solution: The paper clearly articulates limitations of ELBO-based approaches (biased gradients, train/inference mismatch) and proposes an elegant MDP reformulation that enables unbiased stepwise policy optimization
Unbiased gradient estimates: Unlike prior ELBO-based methods, AGRPO provides rigorously proven unbiased updates (Theorem A.1), with tractable stepwise likelihoods for dLLMs

Practical efficiency innovation: The timestep estimation scheme is clever—enabling gradient estimation from k≪m samples rather than forward passes for all m steps, crucial for scaling to hundreds of denoising steps

Strong experimental results: Substantial improvements on Countdown (+12.1%) and Sudoku (+2.1%); unique inference compute/quality frontier analysis showing 4× speedup; consistent outperformance vs. diffu-GRPO, VRPO, SPG across most tasks
Excellent reproducibility: Comprehensive implementation details (Appendix F), clear hyperparameters, standard datasets, promised code, thorough ablations on k, m, µ, unmasking strategy
Variance reduction techniques: Well-motivated entropy importance sampling and low-discrepancy sampling with empirical validation (Figure 4) showing faster convergence
Clear presentation: Well-organized narrative, effective figures (especially Figure 1 comparing three approaches), logical progression from motivation to solution
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Step-level MDP formulation for diffusion RL is not new (DDPO, Flow-GRPO). Adapting to discrete diffusion and scaling via timestep estimation feels incremental; paper could better articulate fundamental novelty beyond applying existing ideas

Mixed empirical results: MATH performance shows only +0.2% improvement with 42.0% accuracy vs. 51.7% for AR models. Paper's speculation about harder tasks/weak priors is unsatisfying and suggests fundamental limitations for harder reasoning

Approximations remain: Stepwise likelihood from parallel token unmasking is product of per-token marginals (not true likelihood); Markovian assumption may not hold for reasoning traces; KL divergence uses k3 estimator. These limit claims of 'unbiasedness' vs. sequence-level objectives

Entropy collapse inadequately addressed: Remark H.1 acknowledges reduced diversity and formulaic answers but relegates this to a remark without systematic study. This could be a serious practical limitation not clearly highlighted
Limited evaluation scope: Only 4 reasoning tasks, all in RLVR setting; no evaluation on other downstream tasks; variance reduction tested on only one task (Countdown)—generalization unclear

Computational cost not fully quantified: Table 6 shows ~20% higher cost per step; Proposition B.1 (cost analysis) is informal with strong assumptions; hardware-dependent bottleneck arguments weaken universal scalability claims

Insufficient ablation on improvement sources: Paper doesn't isolate why AGRPO works—is it the stepwise objective, unbiased gradients, or train/inference alignment? No systematic ablation removing components to test

Train/test mismatch not fully resolved: Uses random unmasking during training (satisfying exogeneity) but confidence-based unmasking at test time (violating assumption). While justified as annealing, represents theoretical inconsistency

Implementation complexity obscures simplicity claims: Requires careful engineering (caching masked states, EOS handling, custom inference, float64 sampling)—Appendix F reveals complexity that could limit adoption despite 'simplicity' in title

Baseline inconsistencies: Reproduced LLaDA-8B-Instruct baselines differ from prior work (Table 2). While consistent parsing is applied, this complicates reproducibility for others and fair comparison with future work
